title: Ephraim McDowell & Jane Todd Crawford (1809)
summary: On Christmas Day 1809 in Danville, Dr. Ephraim McDowell removed a 22.5-pound ovarian tumor from Jane Todd Crawford without anesthesia or antisepsis.
bodyMarkdown:
On Christmas morning in 1809, in his home in [Danville](/stories/danville-and-constitution-square/), Dr. [Ephraim McDowell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ephraim_McDowell) removed a 22.5-pound ovarian tumor from Jane Todd Crawford. It was the first successful removal of an ovarian tumor in the world.

## The surgeon

McDowell was born on November 11, 1771, in Rockbridge County, Virginia, and moved to Kentucky as a boy. He studied with Dr. Alexander Humphreys in Virginia and then [attended lectures at the University of Edinburgh](https://grokipedia.com/page/Ephraim_McDowell) in 1793–94, including those of the surgeon John Bell. He left without a degree and began practicing in Danville in 1795. He became known for removing bladder stones; one patient was a teenage James K. Polk.

## The patient

On December 13, 1809, McDowell was called to see Crawford in Green County. Her physicians thought she was overdue in pregnancy. McDowell diagnosed an ovarian tumor and told her the operation had never been performed. She chose to go ahead and rode to Danville on horseback.

One account puts the distance at 60 miles; [another, on the state historical marker near her home](https://history.ky.gov/markers/jane-todd-crawford), gives sixty-four.

## The operation

The surgery took place without anesthesia or antisepsis, neither of which was yet known. It lasted about 25 minutes. Five days later McDowell found her making up her own bed. She went home after a recovery that one account counts as 25 days and another as four weeks. She lived more than three decades longer.

## A difficult legacy

McDowell did not publish his results until 1817, when [The Eclectic Repertory, vol. 7](https://archive.org/details/eclecticrepertor07phil) carried his report of three cases, Crawford's and two later operations; a second report followed in [vol. 9 (1819)](https://archive.org/details/eclecticrepertor09phil). He performed at least 12 operations for ovarian disease.

He married Sarah Shelby, daughter of Gov. Isaac Shelby, in 1802, and helped found Centre College. He died on June 25, 1830, probably of appendicitis.

## Kentucky today

McDowell is often called the "father of ovariotomy." A monument to him was erected in Danville in 1879. In 1929 a bronze statue of him was placed in the U.S. Capitol's National Statuary Hall, and a stamp honored him in 1959. His Danville home, where the operation took place, is now the [Ephraim McDowell House](https://grokipedia.com/page/ephraim_mcdowell_house) museum and a National Historic Landmark.
